summary: Using CodeScene's proprietary CodeHealth (CH) maintainability score, the authors (two from CodeScene) generate single-shot unit tests with Qwen3-Coder-30B for ~24.6k competitive-programming solutions (5,000 Python, 9,795 Java, 9,825 C++) and correlate CH with line/branch coverage, mutation score, and input-token counts across four tokenizers. They find weak positive CH-effectiveness correlations (strongest for mutation score) and moderate negative CH-token correlations for Java and C++.

claims.claim: CH is a weak but consistent signal of LLM-generated test effectiveness, clearest for mutation score.
claims.evidence: Table II: Spearman rho for mutation score +.18 (Py), +.21 (Java), +.34 (C++); line coverage +.11/+.01(ns)/+.15; partial-for-SLOC Python mutation becomes ns (+.12, only 251 files). Table I Java median mutation 34.8% (CH<6) to 95.1% (CH>=9.8, N=271). Mutation computed only where generated tests passed, a conditioning bias the authors acknowledge.

claims.claim: Lower CH code costs more input tokens, beyond SLOC, for Java and C++.
claims.evidence: Table III: rho -.28 to -.30 (Java), -.25 to -.28 (C++) across Qwen/OpenAI/Claude/Gemini tokenizers; partial-for-SLOC -.24 to -.34; Java persists after controlling for characters (-.25 to -.28). Table I: lowest-CH bin has 45.1% (Java) / 43.8% (C++) higher median tokens than top bin.

claims.claim: AI tools, like humans, perform better on healthy code (practical implication).
claims.evidence: Inferred from correlations on standalone competitive-programming files with one model in single-shot mode; no agentic loop, no industrial code. Authors acknowledge both limits in §V.

patterns.note: Maintainability metric correlates weakly with LLM test effectiveness; suggests static-quality signals matter, but not tested as an in-loop feedback signal.
Quantifies that low-maintainability Java code inflates input tokens ~45% (lowest vs highest CH bin), relevant to context and cost budgets.
Studies LLM unit-test generation (JUnit 5, PIT mutation for Java), single-shot without iteration.

methodology.sample: ~24.6k files from CodeContests (5,000 Python, 9,795 Java, 9,825 C++), stratified by CH with CodeBLEU diversity filter; seven CH bins, sparse at low CH for Python.
methodology.models: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct only, temp 0.1, single shot; four tokenizers for RQ2.
methodology.variance: Single generation per file; Spearman correlations with significance stars; no CIs.
methodology.ablations: Partial correlations controlling for SLOC and character count.
methodology.contamination_controls: None; CodeContests solutions are public and likely in training data.

standards.peer_review: Accepted at SCAM 2026 Engineering Track (arXiv comment).
standards.artifacts: Replication package 'codescene-research/test-generation-scam-2026' with prompt templates; CH metric itself is proprietary CodeScene tooling.

biases.detail: Vendor authors validate their own product's metric (CodeHealth) as predictive of AI performance; CH bin names such as 'AI-ready code' come from the product.
Standalone competitive-programming solutions with stdin/stdout, not production units; acknowledged as main external-validity threat.
Mutation score computed only for files whose generated tests passed; pass rates per CH bin not reported, so selection may drive the mutation trend.
Independent replication of CH scores requires the proprietary CodeScene analyzer.

coi.affiliations: Heidelberg University (student), CodeScene and Lund University (Markus Borg), Lund University, CodeScene (Adam Tornhill).
coi.detail: Two of four authors are from CodeScene, including its founder, and the study favorably positions the company's proprietary metric as an AI-readiness signal, with no independent replication. Mitigating factors: effects are reported candidly as weak, the paper is peer-reviewed, and a replication package exists.

verdict_reason: Large-N, multi-language, peer-reviewed correlational study with honest effect sizes, but a single model in single-shot mode on competitive-programming code, a mutation-score survivorship bias, and a vendor validating its own proprietary metric.
applicability: One of the few papers here with Java numbers. For the work repos, it is weak evidence that refactoring low-maintainability Java (deep nesting, complex methods) before handing it to agents may make generated JUnit tests more effective under PIT mutation testing and reduce input tokens by up to ~45% for the worst files. Any maintainability gate (including open alternatives to CodeScene, consistent with the local-Sonar constituent) is a plausible pre-agent hygiene step. The effects are weak correlations (rho ~0.2 for Java mutation) on toy files with one model and no agent loop, so this should not drive harness architecture. Do not adopt the proprietary metric on this evidence alone.
